n:
- In the spring of the year, the land began to dry out after the heavy winter rains. Kings avoided war during the rainy season.

- David stayed behind either because he was irresponsible in carrying out his royal duties or because he trusted Joab to efficiently handle the Ammonite problem (compare {{2 Samuel 10:7|2 Samuel 10:7}}). This is the first mention of a leader of Israel staying off the battlefield in a time of war.

David’s affair with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah show that David was capable of serious moral failure. These actions deeply damaged David’s life and leadership.

These failures took place during a period when David was enjoying major military success against the Ammonites ({{2 Samuel 10:1-11:1|2 Samuel 10:1–11:1}}; {{2 Samuel 12:26-31|12:26–31}}).

David broke three of the Ten Commandments in these chapters. He wanted his neighbour’s wife Bathsheba.

He committed adultery with her. Then he committed murder by having her husband Uriah killed. According to the Law of Moses, David should have been put to death for these things.

At first David wasn’t sorry for what he had done. Then he heard the story Nathan told about a rich man and a poor man. This story helped David to recognise how he had sinned.

Nathan went on to explain the judgement that David would face for his evil deeds. The son born to him and Bathsheba would die. And there would be terrible trouble in David’s family.

David’s eldest son Amnon caused trouble when he raped his sister Tamar. David did nothing to punish Amnon or to bring justice for Tamar. Then David’s son Absalom caused trouble when he killed Amnon.

David was very sad about this. He avoided seeing Absalom for many years but didn’t take action to punish Absalom.

- *strolled around on the roof*: The roofs of houses were flat and often used for different activities, like drying and storing food ({{Joshua 2:6|Joshua 2:6}}), walking and socializing, and sleeping in warm weather.

- Bathsheba was bathing in clear view from the roof of the king’s palace. She might have thought everyone was inside, escaping the heat or taking a midday rest.

- Bathsheba means "daughter of seven" or "daughter of oath." Her father, Eliam, was the son of Ahithophel (see {{2 Samuel 23:34|2 Samuel 23:34}}), an adviser first to David and then to Absalom ({{2 Samuel 15:12|2 Samuel 15:12}}; {{2 Samuel 16:23|16:23}}). Ahithophel later switched his support from David to Absalom ({{2 Samuel 17:1-4|2 Samuel 17:1–4}}, {{2 Samuel 17:14|14}}), which upset David. He advised Absalom to sleep with David's concubines on a rooftop, where everyone could see ({{2 Samuel 16:20-22|2 Samuel 16:20–22}}). 

- Uriah is a Hebrew name meaning "Yahweh is my light." He might have been a foreign soldier, a convert to the Israelite religion, or an Israelite with Hittite ancestry. Uriah could also have been part of the non-Israelite nobility in Jerusalem before David conquered the city. He was one of David's 30 mightiest warriors ({{2 Samuel 23:39|2 Samuel 23:39}}).

- It is not clear whether Bathsheba came to David’s palace by her own choice. David was the king, and Bathsheba was a subject under his authority. This unequal power relationship means that she may not have been free to refuse his summons.

The text does not record any protest from Bathsheba, unlike other passages where protest is clearly stated (compare {{2 Samuel 13:12-13|2 Samuel 13:12–13}}). Afterward, she married David, bore him another son, and later urged David to name their son as heir ({{1 Kings 1:11-21|1 Kings 1:11–21}}). These details may suggest willing cooperation. 

However, other details point in a different direction. Bathsheba mourned for her husband Uriah ({{2 Samuel 11:26-27|2 Samuel 11:26–27}}), and the text places blame only on David for what happened ({{2 Samuel 11:27|2 Samuel 11:27}}). Given David’s authority and Bathsheba’s vulnerable position, it is also possible that she was taken against her will.

- The phrase about her menstrual period (see {{Leviticus 15:19-24|Leviticus 15:19–24}}) shows that Bathsheba could not have been pregnant by Uriah. It makes clear that the child she conceived must have been David’s.

- *wash your feet*: David assumed that Uriah would have sex with Bathsheba while on this weekend pass. Then everyone except Bathsheba would assume that the child was Uriah’s, conceived on this night. 

- *a gift*: David may not have cared whether Uriah and Bathsheba were actually intimate. If Uriah had gone back to his house, people would have assumed that the pregnancy began during that time. This would have prevented questions about when and how Bathsheba became pregnant.

- *in tents* (Hebrew, *sukkoth*, the name behind *Sukkot,* “the Feast of Tabernacles,” {{Deuteronomy 16:13-17|Deuteronomy 16:13–17}}): These were temporary shelters made of branches and leaves. Soldiers in battle, herders watching their animals, or workers during the grape harvest used these shelters.

- *eat and drink and sleep with my wife?: *Uriah was willing to eat and drink with David ({{2 Samuel 11:13|2 Samuel 11:13}}). What he refused was to sleep with his wife, Bathsheba. In ancient Israel, soldiers on duty treated the camp as a holy place because they believed God was present there to fight for them. For that reason, they avoided anything considered impure, including sexual relations ({{Leviticus 15:18|Leviticus 15:18}}; see also {{1 Samuel 21:5-6|1 Samuel 21:5–6}}).
Uriah was not the only one who died. David sacrificed several other Israelite soldiers while attempting to hide his sin.
*Was it not a woman who dropped an upper millstone on him*: Compare {{Judges 9:54|Judges 9:54}}.
*the sword devours one as well as another*: David spoke as if death in war were random and unavoidable. His words show a cold and careless attitude toward the unnecessary deaths he had caused.

- The Lord sent Nathan to David at least nine months after David committed adultery.

- This account is one of the few places in the Old Testament that uses a parable (a short story that teaches a moral truth; see also {{Judges 9:8-15|Judges 9:8–15}}). Parables can communicate truth in a powerful and indirect way.

- David was rich in many ways. He possessed royal wealth, had many wives, and held God’s promises for his future. By contrast, Uriah was poor. He had one wife, one home, and no continuing family line.
Chapter 12 expands on the final part of {{2 Samuel 11:27|2 Samuel 11:27}}.

*like a daughter*: Nathan compares the lamb to a daughter. The Hebrew word for “daughter” is *bath*. This creates a word connection with Bathsheba’s name, which begins with *bath* (see study note on 2 Samuel 11:3). This comparison strengthens the emotional force of the story and helps David recognize the injustice of his actions.
*he took the poor man’s lamb*: Samuel had previously warned that a king would take what was not his ({{1 Samuel 8:11-17|1 Samuel 8:11–17}}).

The rich man of the parable did not deserve to die according to the law; instead, he must repay four lambs (compare {{Exodus 22:1|Exodus 22:1}}). Interestingly, David later lost four of his sons: 

- Bathsheba’s first child ({{2 Samuel 12:18|2 Samuel 12:18}})

- Amnon ({{2 Samuel 13:29|2 Samuel 13:29}})

- Absalom ({{2 Samuel 18:14-15|2 Samuel 18:14–15}})

- Adonijah ({{1 Kings 2:25|1 Kings 2:25}})

- *You are that man*!: David did deserve to die for his crime ({{Leviticus 20:10|Leviticus 20:10}}).

- *I anointed … I gave … I would have given you*: David's sin broke God's laws against murder, adultery, and coveting ({{Exodus 20:1-17|Exodus 20:1–17}}). It also showed a bold disrespect for everything the Lord had kindly given him.

His wives were likely concubines from Saul’s harem (see {{2 Samuel 3:7|2 Samuel 3:7}}). The phrase might refer to Saul’s wife Ahinoam, but David probably married another woman with the same name (see {{1 Samuel 14:50|1 Samuel 14:50}}; {{1 Samuel 25:43|25:43}}).

- *Now* (literally *forever*): This phrase points to ongoing consequences. It stands in contrast to God’s gracious promises of a lasting kingdom that God gave to David earlier ({{2 Samuel 7:13-29|2 Samuel 7:13–29}}). 

- This is a reminder of what David did with the sword ({{2 Samuel 12:9|2 Samuel 12:9}}) and how *the sword* would affect his family. This recalls David's careless reaction to Joab's report about the deaths of Uriah and other innocent Israelites ({{2 Samuel 11:25|2 Samuel 11:25}}).
*I will raise up adversity against you from your own house*: Absalom's revolt against David fulfilled this promise ({{2 Samuel 14:1-19:43|2 Samuel 14–19}}).

*Nevertheless … the son born to you will surely die*: At times, God allows the consequences of a father’s sin to affect later generations ({{Exodus 20:5|Exodus 20:5}}; {{Exodus 34:7|34:7}}; {{Numbers 14:18|Numbers 14:18}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:9|Deuteronomy 5:9}}; {{Jeremiah 32:18|Jeremiah 32:18}}). Although David repented and God forgave him ({{2 Samuel 12:13|2 Samuel 12:13}}), this forgiveness did not remove all consequences. Instead, the punishment was delayed and carried forward into a later generation (see {{1 Kings 21:27-29|1 Kings 21:27–29}}).
The series of actions described here show David resuming normal life activities. That he did so this soon after his son’s death amazed his advisers s ({{2 Samuel 12:21|2 Samuel 12:21}}).
David mourned and fasted before his son died, hoping that God would remove the punishment.

*Can I bring him back again? I will go to him*: The finality of his son’s death forced David to face his own mortality. At the same time, his words express confidence that life continues after death and that he would one day join his son.

- Even after Uriah's death, Bathsheba was still referred to as Uriah's wife ({{2 Samuel 12:9|2 Samuel 12:9}}; see also {{Matthew 1:6|Matthew 1:6}}). Only here is she called David's wife. 

- *Solomon*: In Hebrew, Solomon’s name is pronounced *Shelomoh*. It likely means “his peace,” from the Hebrew word *shalom* (peace).

The name may also mean “his replacement.” This meaning comes from the Hebrew root *shelem*, which can mean “replacement” or “compensation.” Similar names include *Shelemiah* ({{Jeremiah 36:14|Jeremiah 36:14}}), which means “Yahweh has provided compensation,” and *Shelumiel* ({{Numbers 1:6|Numbers 1:6}}), which means “God is my compensation.” Both meanings fit the context of Solomon’s birth after the loss of David and Bathsheba’s first child.

*Jedidiah* means “loved by Yahweh.” This second name, which God gave to Solomon, appears only here in the Bible. It expresses God’s special love for him and points to God’s intention to secure Solomon’s future.
David's fight with the Ammonites, which began in {{2 Samuel 10:1-19|2 Samuel 10}}, ended in success.

- *he took the crown*: By taking the crown, David effectively showed that he now ruled over the Ammonites, as if he had become their king.

- *a great amount of plunder*: The law warned Israel not to take certain kinds of war booty during conquest because of its danger ({{Deuteronomy 7:25-26|Deuteronomy 7:25–26}}). The wealth David took was dangerous. Riches could turn his heart away from God if he trusted them instead of the Lord.

He also enslaved the people of Rabbah, forcing them to work. Enslaving defeated peoples followed the rules in {{Deuteronomy 20:11|Deuteronomy 20:11}}. Solomon later did the same with the Canaanites ({{1 Kings 9:20-22|1 Kings 9:20–22}}; see also {{Judges 1:30|Judges 1:30}}, {{Judges 1:33|33}}). Another interpretation suggests the defeated Ammonites were tortured (compare {{1 Chronicles 20:3|textual note on 1 Chronicles 20:3}}).

*the beautiful sister*: Tamar was the full sister of Absalom, but only the half sister of Amnon (see {{2 Samuel 3:2-3|2 Samuel 3:2–3}}). As Tamar’s closest male relative, Absalom later took action to avenge her ({{2 Samuel 13:23-29|2 Samuel 13:23–29}}; compare {{Genesis 34:1-31|Genesis 34}}; {{Numbers 35:19|Numbers 35:19}}).

- *sick with frustration*: The story shows that Amnon's "love" for Tamar ({{2 Samuel 13:4|2 Samuel 13:4}}) was not healthy love. It was an unhealthy sexual obsession that made him emotionally distressed.

- *She was a virgin*: Amnon’s fixation grew stronger because Tamar had not had sexual relations.

- *it seemed implausible for him to do anything to her*: The law forbade marriage between a brother and a sister ({{Leviticus 18:9|Leviticus 18:9}}, {{Leviticus 18:11|11}}; {{Leviticus 20:17|20:17}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:22|Deuteronomy 27:22}}). However, Amnon did not seek marriage with Tamar. He wanted only to have sex with her.

- *shrewd* (literally *wise*): Jonadab's "wisdom" was similar to the serpent's cleverness ({{Genesis 3:1|Genesis 3:1}}). 

- In the context of a royal court, the Hebrew term for friend is closer to “counselor” or “adviser.”
*morning after morning*: Amnon's obsession grew stronger and never stopped.

- *disgraceful thing*: The Hebrew word *nebalah* means "outrage" or "deplorable act." It often refers to sexual crimes like rape and adultery ({{Genesis 34:7|Genesis 34:7}}; {{Deuteronomy 22:21|Deuteronomy 22:21}}; {{Judges 20:6|Judges 20:6}}, {{Judges 20:10|10}}; {{Jeremiah 29:23|Jeremiah 29:23}}). The person responsible must pay with his life. 

- *in Israel*: The added phrase either shows outrage that such a crime took place among Israelites, or it describes the act as a serious violation of Israel’s standards for sexual behavior.
*he will not withhold me from you*: Tamar said this to gain time. Amnon knew that the law prohibited marriage between half-siblings (see study note on 2 Samuel 13:2), and he refused to stop.
*being stronger*: Tamar resisted as much as she could.
The fact that Amnon’s feelings for Tamar quickly changed into hate shows that what he called “love” ({{2 Samuel 13:4|2 Samuel 13:4}}) was actually selfish sexual desire, not genuine care for her.

*worse than this great wrong you have already done*: In that culture, a virgin who had been raped was considered unable to marry ({{2 Samuel 13:20|2 Samuel 13:20}}; see {{Deuteronomy 22:28-29|Deuteronomy 22:28–29}}).
*a robe of many colors*: This phrase also describes Joseph's robe in {{Genesis 37:3|Genesis 37:3}}.

- Tamar tore her robe to show the loss of her virginity and honor and to mourn her future's end ({{2 Samuel 13:16|2 Samuel 13:16}}).

- Ashes symbolized death; sitting in ashes or placing ashes on one's head were signs of mourning ({{Esther 4:1-3|Esther 4:1–3}}; {{Job 42:6|Job 42:6}}; {{Daniel 9:3|Daniel 9:3}}; {{Jonah 3:6|Jonah 3:6}}).

- *Be quiet for now … Do not take this thing to heart*: Absalom’s words sound comforting, but they do not match Tamar’s deep shame and grief. This restrained response hid Absalom’s intense anger ({{2 Samuel 13:22|2 Samuel 13:22}}) from Tamar, who was already overwhelmed.

- *as a desolate woman*: See study note on 2 Samuel 13:16.

*King David … was furious*: David was deeply angry about what happened, but he does not seem to have punished Amnon.

Some ancient texts, including the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek version, add an explanation. They say David did not punish Amnon because he loved him. Another possibility is that David, who had committed sexual sin himself (see {{2 Samuel 11:1-12:24|2 Samuel 11:1–12:24}}), felt unable to judge his son for a similar offense. A third possibility is that David saw this event as a form of God’s “eye for an eye” judgment for his own wrongdoing.

- Baal-hazor is different from the well-known fortified city of Hazor, which is north of the Sea of Galilee. A fortified city is a city protected by strong walls and defenses. Baal-hazor is believed to be at Jebel el-Asur, about 24 kilometers (15 miles) north of Jerusalem.

- *he invited all the sons of the king*: Sheep shearing was a time to share abundance and blessings with others (see {{1 Samuel 25:2-8|1 Samuel 25:2–8}}).
David tore his robe, just like Tamar did after being harmed ({{2 Samuel 13:19|2 Samuel 13:19}}). This act showed deep distress or regret (see also {{Genesis 37:34|Genesis 37:34}}).
Absalom was now a fugitive. He sought refuge among his mother’s family.

- *fled and went to Talmai*: See {{2 Samuel 3:3|2 Samuel 3:3}}.

- Geshur was in Aram, northeast of Israel’s territory (see {{2 Samuel 15:8|2 Samuel 15:8}}; {{Joshua 13:13|Joshua 13:13}}).

- *And King David*: The Dead Sea Scrolls and Greek version say *And the spirit of the king.* 

- *longed to go to Absalom*: David’s intense grief over Amnon’s death had eased. Any desire he may have had to put Absalom to death had faded, and he now wanted to restore their relationship.
The woman with a reputation for great wisdom was summoned to carry out a delicate mission in the royal court (compare {{2 Samuel 20:16|2 Samuel 20:16}}).
*My lord the king, may any blame be on me*: If David allowed a murder to go unpunished, he would fail to uphold justice and would likely be criticized by the people.

*As surely as the LORD lives*: When the woman urged David to promise more protection, he responded with this solemn oath (see {{2 Samuel 4:9|2 Samuel 4:9}}; {{2 Samuel 12:5|12:5}}; {{2 Samuel 15:21|15:21}}; {{1 Samuel 20:3|1 Samuel 20:3}}; {{1 Samuel 28:10|28:10}}; {{1 Samuel 29:6|29:6}}).

*against the people of God*: The woman argued that David was harming the entire kingdom by keeping Absalom in exile. She suggested that conflict in the royal family would spread to the wider society, or that David’s focus on Absalom would distract him from ruling well ({{2 Samuel 14:16|2 Samuel 14:16}}).

*God … devises ways*: The woman encouraged David to make peace with Absalom, just as God does with his people. God did not stay distant from David when he sinned. He forgave the king when he repented.

- The woman again spoke about her own case. She argued that the king’s concern for Absalom kept him from addressing justice among his people (see {{2 Samuel 13:39|2 Samuel 13:39}} and study note on 2 Samuel 13:39).

- *cut off both*: If her only remaining son were killed, her family would lose its ancestral land (compare {{Numbers 27:1-11|Numbers 27:1–11}}).

*just like the angel of God*: This expression shows great respect. It is not used for anyone else in the Bible and appears four times in reference to David (see also {{2 Samuel 14:20|2 Samuel 14:20}}; {{2 Samuel 19:27|19:27}}; {{1 Samuel 29:9|1 Samuel 29:9}}). The woman was expressing confidence that David would act with wisdom and justice given by God.
*has wisdom like the wisdom of the angel of God*: This wise woman ({{2 Samuel 14:2|2 Samuel 14:2}}) knew it was better to praise a king than to insult him.
*bring back … Absalom*: It seems that David was not yet interested in full reconciliation with his son ({{2 Samuel 14:24|2 Samuel 14:24}}).
*he shaved it every year*: Absalom's hair, which made him attractive, became a deadly trap for him (see {{2 Samuel 18:9-15|2 Samuel 18:9–15}}).

- Absalom's three sons likely died before him (see {{2 Samuel 18:18|2 Samuel 18:18}}).

- Absalom named his daughter Tamar after his sister, and she was also very beautiful ({{2 Samuel 13:1|2 Samuel 13:1}}).

Joab persuaded David to welcome Absalom back ({{2 Samuel 14:21-22|2 Samuel 14:21–22}}). However, he then stopped helping Absalom, possibly to avoid supporting someone who might try to take the throne ({{2 Samuel 15:1-12|2 Samuel 15:1–12}}).

- Absalom bowed deeply, showing respect to the king (see also {{2 Samuel 14:4|2 Samuel 4:4}}, {{2 Samuel 14:22|22}}). 

- *the king kissed Absalom*: The absence of talking, hugging (compare {{Luke 15:20|Luke 15:20}}), or crying (compare {{Genesis 33:4|Genesis 33:4}}; {{Genesis 45:2|45:2}}, {{Genesis 45:14|14}}) suggests this was a formal meeting, not an affectionate reunion.

*a chariot with horses and fifty men*: These items were clear signs of kingship. Samuel warned that a king would take these from the people ({{1 Samuel 8:11|1 Samuel 8:11}}). David's son, Adonijah, also gathered these when he wanted to be king ({{1 Kings 1:5|1 Kings 1:5}}).

Absalom revolted against David eleven years after Amnon violated Tamar (compare {{2 Samuel 13:23|2 Samuel 13:23}}, {{2 Samuel 13:38|38}}; {{2 Samuel 14:28|14:28}}; {{2 Samuel 15:7|15:7}}). This was around the twenty-fifth year of David's thirty-three-year rule in Jerusalem.

Absalom continued to cause trouble in David’s family. He didn’t honour God’s choice of David as the king. Absalom wanted to make himself king while David was still alive. He hadn’t been chosen by God or anointed by a prophet to be king. But he convinced many Israelites to follow him.

He made plans to kill his father and he had sex with David’s concubines. This was a way to show that he had more authority in Jerusalem than David did. It also fulfilled part of Nathan’s prophecy against David for committing adultery and murder.

As David ran away from Absalom, he made careful plans. He received help from people who remained faithful to him. David also prayed (prayer) to God for help. David didn’t want to punish those who spoke against him. Instead he trusted God to provide the covenant blessings for him.

Even though Absalom had become David’s enemy, David didn’t celebrate when Absalom was killed. After that, David returned to Jerusalem to continue ruling as king.
Bowing before Absalom was to honor him as king (see {{2 Samuel 14:33|2 Samuel 14:33}}).
Absalom welcomed the people and acted as if he cared about them. In this way, he won their loyalty through false concern.

- *After four years*: The Hebrew text says *forty years,* which would place Absalom’s rebellion in David’s final year as king, causing many timeline issues with later events (also see study note on 2 Samuel 15:1–19). The Greek and Syriac versions are more likely accurate. 

- *fulfill a vow*: This offering was to keep a promise to God, unlike a freewill offering given out of devotion and gratitude (see {{Genesis 28:20-22|Genesis 28:20–22}}; {{Judges 11:30-31|Judges 11:30–31}}; {{1 Samuel 1:11|1 Samuel 1:11}}). Absalom was probably lying (compare {{1 Samuel 20:28-29|1 Samuel 20:28–29}}).

- *Geshur of Aram*: After killing Amnon, Absalom had sought refuge in the homeland of his mother (see study notes on 2 Samuel 13:34–39, 37).

- Hebron, David's first capital, was the ideal place for Absalom to turn his local popularity into a full revolt against David.

- Ahithophel was Bathsheba’s grandfather (see {{2 Samuel 11:3|2 Samuel 11:3}}; {{2 Samuel 23:34|23:34}}). Years later, he might have still been upset about David's actions toward his granddaughter. 

- Giloh was located in the region of Hebron ({{Joshua 15:51|Joshua 15:51}}, {{Joshua 15:54|54}}).
David might have left ten of his concubines behind because he thought his exile would be brief. See {{2 Samuel 16:21-22|2 Samuel 16:21–22}}.

- *six hundred Gittites*: This alliance began with David's connection to the Philistines during Saul's time ({{1 Samuel 21:10-15|1 Samuel 21:10–15}}; {{1 Samuel 27:1-12|27:1–12}}; {{1 Samuel 29:1-11|29:1–11}}).

- *the Cherethites and Pelethites*: Refer to the study note on 2 Samuel 8:18.

- Ittai was a Philistine from Gath. He was associated with Gibeah in Benjamin ({{2 Samuel 23:29|2 Samuel 23:29}}; {{1 Chronicles 11:31|1 Chronicles 11:31}}). The Philistines had set up a military post in Gibeah at the start of Saul's rule ({{1 Samuel 10:5|1 Samuel 10:5}}; {{1 Samuel 13:3|13:3}}). 

- David was stepping aside for King Absalom, who had gained the loyalty of the people of Israel.
The Kidron Valley, east of Jerusalem, separated the City of David from the Mount of Olives.

Zadok was one of two priests who served King David ({{2 Samuel 8:17|2 Samuel 8:17}}). He later anointed Solomon as king ({{1 Kings 1:39|1 Kings 1:39}}) and became the high priest after Abiathar lost his position ({{1 Kings 2:26-27|1 Kings 2:26–27}}).

*Return the ark of God*: When people fled invasions, they usually took their idols to prevent enemies from capturing them. If a god was captured, rebels might think the gods had abandoned the ruling family. However, the ark was not just an idol or charm (compare {{1 Samuel 4:3-11|1 Samuel 4:3–11}}; {{1 Samuel 5:6-6:9|5:6–6:9}}). It was the main object in the sanctuary and symbolized the presence of the Lord, the God of Israel (see {{Exodus 40:34-35|Exodus 40:34–35}}). David allowed the ark to fall into Absalom’s hands on purpose, trusting in God’s grace and promises ({{2 Samuel 15:26|2 Samuel 15:26}}; see {{2 Samuel 7:8-16|7:8–16}}) whether or not the ark was with him.
Ahimaaz and Jonathan supported David during Absalom’s rebellion by serving as secret messengers (see {{2 Samuel 15:36|2 Samuel 15:36}}; {{2 Samuel 17:17-22|17:17–22}}).

*turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness*: David also sent Hushai, who pretended to support Absalom while secretly serving David. Hushai worked to confuse and undermine Ahithophel’s advice ({{2 Samuel 15:32-37|2 Samuel 15:32–37}}; {{2 Samuel 17:1-14|17:1–14}}).

- At this point in Israel’s history, people worshiped God at multiple altars across the land. The tabernacle, which had been around since the time of Joshua and Samuel, no longer existed. The temple had not yet been built.

- An Arkite was possibly a non-Israelite from the region south of Bethel ({{Joshua 16:2|Joshua 16:2}}).
David believed God was guiding events, but he also made strategic moves to support his goals.

- *Ziba*: See study note on 2 Samuel 9:11; also see {{2 Samuel 9:1-13|2 Samuel 9:1–13}}; {{2 Samuel 19:24-30|19:24–30}}.

- As Saul’s grandson ({{2 Samuel 16:3|2 Samuel 16:3}}), Mephibosheth was a potential rival for the throne.
Ziba was lying to David for his own benefit. Later, Mephibosheth told the truth about what happened ({{2 Samuel 19:24-30|2 Samuel 19:24–30}}).

Bahurim was in the territory of Benjamin, east of the Mount of Olives, on the road to the Jordan River. Many people from Benjamin, the tribe of Saul, likely still felt resentment toward David’s rule. In Shimei’s case, this loyalty to Saul was even stronger because Shimei belonged to Saul’s own clan within the tribe of Benjamin.
Shimei cursed David. He blamed David for the violent deaths of Saul and members of Saul’s family.
*The LORD has paid you back*: Shimei thought Absalom's rebellion was the Lord punishing David. However, David was innocent (see study notes on 2 Samuel 1:4, 15–16).

Abishai was David’s nephew ({{1 Chronicles 2:13-16|1 Chronicles 2:13–16}}) and likely part of his personal guard. He thought no one should speak to the king disrespectfully and survive (compare {{2 Samuel 19:21|2 Samuel 19:21}}). David was more cautious in making judgments (compare {{1 Kings 2:8-9|1 Kings 2:8–9}}).

- *If he curses me because the LORD told him*: David thought it might be punishment for past sins. 

- David was actually reducing the violence around him, despite Shimei's accusations.
*How much more*: David understood why someone who supported Saul might hate him.

*Long live the king!*: Hushai's words were intentionally unclear. He was actually serving the true king, David, who was truly "the one chosen by the LORD" ({{2 Samuel 16:18|2 Samuel 16:18}}). Hushai avoided mentioning the king's name, making Absalom think Hushai was loyal to him instead of David.

*whom should I serve*: (literally *and second, to whom will I do service? Not before his son?*): The unclear language continues. Hushai expressed his loyalty as a question, not a promise. He intended to serve David while tricking Absalom into believing he had switched sides. Similarly, *As I served in your father’s presence, so also I will serve in yours* literally means, *as I served before your father, so I will* [serve your father] *before you.*

*Sleep with your father's concubines*: A usurper (someone who takes power by force) would take a previous ruler's harem to strengthen his claim to the throne (see {{2 Samuel 3:7|2 Samuel 3:7}}). Absalom's action violated {{Deuteronomy 22:30|Deuteronomy 22:30}}.

Absalom wanted to show the people he had taken the throne and its royal powers. His disgraceful act mirrored David’s affair with Bathsheba, which also started on that roof ({{2 Samuel 11:2-4|2 Samuel 11:2–4}}). This event fulfilled Nathan’s prophecy ({{2 Samuel 12:11-12|2 Samuel 12:11–12}}).
*was like the consultation of the word of God*: Compare with {{2 Samuel 17:14|2 Samuel 17:14}}.

Ahithophel advised a quick surprise attack against David with a small force of 12,000 men ({{2 Samuel 17:1|2 Samuel 17:1}}). This plan would give David no time to prepare or organize a defense.

David’s double agent, Hushai, gave different advice. He urged Absalom to wait and gather the entire army of Israel before attacking ({{2 Samuel 17:11|2 Samuel 17:11}}). This plan promised a much larger force and would prevent David from using guerrilla tactics (small surprise attacks).

Because the Lord was working against Absalom, he rejected Ahithophel’s good advice and accepted Hushai’s poor advice ({{2 Samuel 17:14|2 Samuel 17:14}}; compare {{1 Kings 12:1-15|1 Kings 12:1–15}}).
*as a bride … You seek*: The Hebrew text suggests that everyone's loyalty depends on David's death. The Greek version shows a young wife returning to her husband after a brief argument.
The nationwide military draft from Dan to Beersheba (the northern and southern limits of Israel) aimed to create a much stronger army.

- Ahithophel’s strategy was the stronger military plan. However, Hushai had a psychological and rhetorical advantage (he understood how to persuade Absalom). He also carried out the Lord’s purpose. Because of this, Hushai gained Absalom’s favor.

- *the LORD had purposed to thwart*: Although Absalom made early gains, his attempt to take the throne was doomed from the beginning.

- *Jonathan and Ahimaaz*: See {{2 Samuel 15:27|2 Samuel 15:27}}, {{2 Samuel 15:36|36}}. 

- The location of En-rogel is uncertain, but it cannot have been too far east of Jerusalem.

Bahurim was where Shimei, a supporter of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin, lived ({{2 Samuel 16:5|2 Samuel 16:5}}; {{2 Samuel 19:16|19:16}}). Shimei’s cursing of David at Bahurim showed David’s decline. In contrast, the escape of Ahimaaz and Jonathan showed hope for David’s return to power.
*hanged himself*: Ahithophel saw that David would win and Absalom would fail. He chose to take his own life instead of facing David.
Mahanaim was once the capital city of Ish-bosheth and Abner ({{2 Samuel 2:8|2 Samuel 2:8}}, {{2 Samuel 2:12|12}}, {{2 Samuel 2:29|29}}). It later became the base from which David ruled.

According to {{1 Chronicles 2:15-16|1 Chronicles 2:15–16}}, Abigail and Zeruiah were David’s sisters. However, since Abigail is called the daughter of Nahash, they were likely David’s half-sisters. Nahash was probably their father, and his widow may have married Jesse, who then had David and his brothers.

- Shobi was probably the brother of Hanun, who had humiliated David’s messengers after the death of Nahash ({{2 Samuel 10:1-19|2 Samuel 10}}; see study note on 2 Samuel 10:1–5).

- Makir was Mephibosheth’s host before David summoned him ({{2 Samuel 9:4-5|2 Samuel 9:4–5}}). 

- Barzillai of Gilead was probably not the same as Barzillai from Meholah ({{2 Samuel 21:8|2 Samuel 21:8}}).

*you are worth ten thousand of us*: David's men praised him, but their request for him to stay behind might actually suggest that David was becoming weaker (see {{2 Samuel 21:15-17|2 Samuel 21:15–17}}).

Joab disobeyed David's order to be gentle with young Absalom ({{2 Samuel 18:11-15|2 Samuel 18:11–15}}). This was the second time Joab killed someone against David's wishes (see {{2 Samuel 3:22-37|2 Samuel 3:22–37}}).
The forest of Ephraim was an area east of the Jordan settled by the tribe of Ephraim.
*the forest devoured more people*: The land in the forest (its rough ground and thick growth) removed the numerical advantage of Absalom’s army.

Absalom, who was very proud of his hair, died because of it. He had *set up for himself a pillar* ({{2 Samuel 18:18|2 Samuel 18:18}}), but after his death, he was thrown into a pit ({{2 Samuel 18:17|2 Samuel 18:17}}) and did not receive a proper burial. These contrasts highlight the difference between Absalom’s goals and his final outcome.
A hero's belt might have been a sword belt that honored a soldier for bravery and courage in battle (compare {{1 Samuel 18:4|1 Samuel 18:4}}).

*thrust them through the heart of Absalom*: Earlier, Joab acted as a peacemaker between David and Absalom ({{2 Samuel 14:1-33|2 Samuel 14}}). Joab might have thought letting Absalom live would cause more problems for David and himself. (Absalom had chosen Amasa, Joab’s first cousin, to take Joab’s place as the commander of Israel’s army; see {{2 Samuel 17:25|2 Samuel 17:25}}.)
*surrounded … and killed him*: Perhaps Joab ordered his armor bearers to kill Absalom. In this way, Joab could later argue to David that he himself did not kill Absalom.

*all the Israelites fled, each to his home*: Those who supported Absalom knew their lives were in danger ({{2 Samuel 17:11|2 Samuel 17:11}}; compare {{2 Samuel 19:8|2 Samuel 19:8}}). They had supported a usurper (a person who tried to take the throne by force), and his attempt to seize the kingdom had failed.

- *I have no son*: See study note on 2 Samuel 14:27. Because Absalom had no heir to continue his family line, he hoped a monument would keep his name and memory alive. 

- *to this day*: The narrator was probably writing during the reign of Solomon. The location of the monument is now unknown.
*A Cushite*: Joab decided it was safer to send a foreigner to inform the king about Absalom's death. If David reacted badly, losing a foreigner was less significant than losing a priest's son.
*If he is alone … he bears good news*: A runner traveling alone was usually a messenger who carried official news.

*All is well!* (Hebrew *shalom* [peace, safety, well-being]): David then asked, “Is the young man Ab-*shalom shalom*? (That is, “What about young Absalom? Is he all right?”) Even though Absalom had opposed him, he was still David’s son. David cared more about his son’s fate than about the well-being of the soldiers who had fought for him ({{2 Samuel 19:5-6|2 Samuel 19:5–6}}).
David was not afraid to show his emotions openly, whether filled with great joy ({{2 Samuel 6:14-19|2 Samuel 6:14–19}}) or deep sadness. His feelings for Absalom were genuine, not fake.
These verses record the only time that Joab openly corrected David (compare {{2 Samuel 24:3|2 Samuel 24:3}}).

The argument among the tribes of Israel (possibly only the northern tribes) led them to agree that they should ask David to return as king. They may have preferred this option instead of returning to a time of weak shared leadership (the period of the judges; see {{2 Samuel 20:1|2 Samuel 20:1}}).

When David saw that the northern tribes would accept him ({{2 Samuel 19:9-10|2 Samuel 19:9–10}}), he sent messengers to encourage Judah, his own people, to accept him too. See also study note on 2 Samuel 19:41–43.
*Commander … in place of Joab*: Amasa did not hold this position for long (see {{2 Samuel 20:7-10|2 Samuel 20:7–10}}).
Gilgal was an important city during the time of Samuel and Saul (see study note on 2 Samuel 19:40; {{1 Samuel 7:16|1 Samuel 7:16}}; {{1 Samuel 11:15|11:15}}).

When David returned to Jerusalem, he forgave Shimei. Shimei was a supporter of Saul who had cursed David during his escape (see {{2 Samuel 16:5-14|2 Samuel 16:5–14}}). However, Shimei's actions were eventually punished ({{1 Kings 2:8|1 Kings 2:8}}, {{1 Kings 2:36-46|36–46}}).

- *your servant knows that I have sinned*: Shimei might have truly repented, or he might have been trying to save his life. David's concern for Absalom's safety showed he was not the ruthless throne-stealer Shimei thought. Absalom did not replace David ({{2 Samuel 16:8|2 Samuel 16:8}}), as Shimei claimed. 

- *all the house of Joseph*: Just as Jacob's name could represent all Israel (for example, {{Numbers 24:19|Numbers 24:19}}; {{Isaiah 10:20|Isaiah 10:20}}), Joseph's name could represent all the northern tribes (see study notes on Amos 5:6; Zechariah 10:6).

- Compare {{2 Samuel 16:9-12|2 Samuel 16:9–12}}.

- *Abishai*: See study note on 2 Samuel 16:9. 

- *Sons of Zeruiah*: See study notes on 2 Samuel 2:18; 17:25. Abishai often wanted to kill those against David (compare {{2 Samuel 16:9|2 Samuel 16:9}}; {{1 Samuel 26:8|1 Samuel 26:8}}). David was also frustrated with Joab, Abishai’s brother (see {{2 Samuel 3:28-29|2 Samuel 3:28–29}}, {{2 Samuel 3:39|39}}; {{2 Samuel 19:13|19:13}}; {{1 Kings 2:5-6|1 Kings 2:5–6}}).
David’s oath of protection was not binding on David’s heir, Solomon, who later ordered Shimei’s execution for far less serious crimes ({{1 Kings 2:36-46|1 Kings 2:36–46}}).

Mephibosheth did not care for his appearance while David was away from Jerusalem. This lack of grooming was a sign of mourning and showed his loyalty to David. If Mephibosheth had planned to claim the throne ({{2 Samuel 16:3|2 Samuel 16:3}}), he would not have kept such an unkempt appearance.

- *like the angel of God*: See study note on 2 Samuel 14:17.

- *deserves death … What further right, then, do I have to keep appealing?*: If Mephibosheth had wanted to betray David, it would have shown deep ingratitude for all David had done for him.
Mephibosheth's lack of interest in claiming half of his property clearly showed his true happiness about David's return.
Gilead was part of Manasseh’s territory on the east side of the Jordan ({{Joshua 17:5|Joshua 17:5}}).

Barzillai was old and weak, so he turned down David's invitation to the royal court in Jerusalem. This invitation was a reward for Barzillai's help. Instead, David took Barzillai’s son Kimham (see also {{1 Kings 2:7|1 Kings 2:7}}).

*kissed Barzillai*: This kiss was sincere and showed real affection. It contrasts with David’s cold kiss for Absalom ({{2 Samuel 14:33|2 Samuel 14:33}}) and with Absalom’s planned kiss to win the people’s favor ({{2 Samuel 15:5|2 Samuel 15:5}}).

Gilgal, a natural stop along David’s westward route, was also a politically significant location: It was where the people had proclaimed Saul king ({{1 Samuel 11:15|1 Samuel 11:15}}) and where Samuel later announced Saul's reign would end ({{1 Samuel 13:13-15|1 Samuel 13:13–15}}). David’s kingship now had a new beginning at Gilgal.

- This disagreement started because David favored his own tribe, Judah. It shows the early signs of the split that eventually divided Judah and Israel into two nations ({{1 Kings 11:31|1 Kings 11:31}}; {{1 Kings 12:16|12:16}}, {{1 Kings 12:20|20}}).

- *Were we not the first*: See {{2 Samuel 19:11-12|2 Samuel 19:11–12}}.

*We have no share in David*: The northern Israelites used this same rallying cry to break away from Solomon ({{1 Kings 12:16|1 Kings 12:16}}). Sheba’s failed revolt hinted at the eventual downfall of the northern kingdom, which began with a similar revolt by Jeroboam ({{1 Kings 12:1-33|1 Kings 12}}).

The ten concubines ({{2 Samuel 15:16|2 Samuel 15:16}}) whom Absalom had publicly mistreated ({{2 Samuel 16:21-22|16:21–22}}) faced a fate similar to Michal’s (see{{2 Samuel 6:23|6:23}} and 2 Samuel 6:23).
The king made Amasa the new commander of the armies, replacing Joab ({{2 Samuel 19:13-14|2 Samuel 19:13–14}}). David expected Amasa to be as efficient and effective as Joab.
*the Cherethites, the Pelethites*: See study note on 2 Samuel 8:18.
*to kiss him*: This was a common greeting that showed respect and warmth. However, such greetings were not always sincere (compare {{2 Samuel 14:33|2 Samuel 14:33}}).

*Amasa … died*: This was the second time Joab killed an enemy commander through deceit. The first was Abner ({{2 Samuel 3:26-27|2 Samuel 3:26–27}}). David tried twice to unite enemy groups by including the enemy's military leader ({{2 Samuel 3:6-13|2 Samuel 3:6–13}}; {{2 Samuel 17:25|17:25}}; {{2 Samuel 19:13|19:13}}). Both times, Joab ruined David's plans by deceitfully murdering the rival commander ({{2 Samuel 3:22-30|2 Samuel 3:22–30}}).
Abel-beth-maacah was in the northernmost region of Israelite territory, 6.4 kilometers (4 miles) west of Dan.
A siege ramp was usually a dirt ramp constructed against a wall. It was a common method to break through a city's defenses (see also {{2 Kings 25:1|2 Kings 25:1}}; {{Jeremiah 52:4|Jeremiah 52:4}}).

- The woman shared a saying to persuade Joab not to destroy the entire city, especially a noble one like Abel (short for Abel-beth-maacah, {{2 Samuel 20:15|2 Samuel 20:15}}), just to catch one criminal.

- *a city that is a mother in Israel*: It was common to refer to outlying villages around a larger city as its “daughters.”
In {{2 Samuel 8:16|2 Samuel 8:16}}, Joab was said to be "over the army," but here he is the commander of Israel's army. David gained full control of Israel after defeating the northern rebel groups.

This list of David’s leaders and the similar list in {{2 Samuel 8:15-18|2 Samuel 8:15–18}} marks the beginning and end of chapters {{2 Samuel 9:1-20:26|9–20}} in David’s life. Even after the major crises described in these 12 chapters, David’s rule did not collapse. He still had a complete and functioning administration.

*Adoram*: The officer in charge of forced labor (not mentioned in {{2 Samuel 8:15-18|2 Samuel:15–18}}; see also {{1 Kings 4:6|1 Kings 4:6}}). This indicates that David now controlled Israel enough to collect taxes and slave labor across the kingdom (compare {{1 Samuel 8:11-17|1 Samuel 8:11–17}}).
Unlike David's personal priest (see {{2 Samuel 8:18|2 Samuel 8:18}}; {{2 Samuel 20:26|20:26}} and corresponding notes), Zadok and Abiathar led public worship.
David’s personal priest was probably not a Levite but rather a special class of religious servant appointed for his royal court (see study note on 2 Samuel 8:18).
